target:
Blepharitis can lead to other eye problems, including:
- Stye. A stye is a red, painful bump on the eyelid caused by a blocked oil gland.
- Chalazion. A chalazion is a hard, painless lump on the eyelid caused by a blocked oil gland. Often, this happens when you have a stye that doesn’t go away. It can make your eyelid swell and turn red. A chalazion will often go away on its own.
- Dry eye. Oil and flakes can build up in your tear film (a thin layer of tears across the surface of your eye). This can make your eyes feel dry. Or your eyes may feel watery or teary because your tears aren’t working correctly.
- Damage to the cornea. In severe cases, blepharitis can hurt your cornea (the clear outer layer at the front of your eye). This can happen because of swelling or irritation in your eyelids or eye lashes that grow in the wrong direction.
- Chronic (long-term) red eye. Blepharitis can make the white part of your eye look red all the time [nei_007_chunk_04].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

How often you need to get a dilated eye exam depends on your risk for eye disease [nei_028_chunk_01]. If you’re over age 60, African American and over age 40, or have a family history of glaucoma, get it every 1 to 2 years [nei_028_chunk_01]. Most people with diabetes or high blood pressure need it at least once a year [nei_028_chunk_01]. If you’re at higher risk, you need a comprehensive dilated eye exam every 1 to 2 years [nei_002_chunk_03].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

No. Farsightedness (hyperopia) and presbyopia are not the same thing [nei_013_chunk_02].

Farsightedness is a refractive error where nearby objects appear blurry [nei_011_chunk_02]. It happens when the eyeball is too short or the cornea and lens shape is abnormal, causing light to focus behind the retina [nei_011_chunk_02].

Presbyopia is an age-related condition where the lens hardens and loses flexibility [nei_013_chunk_02]. This makes it hard to focus on nearby objects [nei_013_chunk_02].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.
target:
No. Presbyopia is different than farsightedness — another refractive error that makes it hard to see things up close [nei_013_chunk_02]. As you age, the lens in your eye gets harder and less flexible, and it stops focusing light correctly on the retina [nei_013_chunk_02]. Most people who are farsighted are born with it, but it may not cause vision problems until you get older [nei_011_chunk_02].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

It happens when the shape of the eye makes light focus behind the retina (a light sensitive layer of the eye), instead of on it [nei_048_chunk_02]. This can be caused by an eyeball that grows too short from front to back, or by problems with the shape of the cornea or lens [nei_011_chunk_02].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

Eye doctors can check for RP as part of a comprehensive dilated eye exam [nei_020_chunk_03]. The exam is simple and painless — the doctor will give you some eye drops to dilate (widen) your pupil and then check your eyes for RP and other eye problems [nei_020_chunk_03].

This exam includes a visual field test to check peripheral (side) vision [nei_020_chunk_03].

Other tests for RP include:
- Electroretinography (ERG) [nei_020_chunk_03].
- Optical coherence tomography (OCT) [nei_020_chunk_03].
- Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging [nei_020_chunk_03].
- Genetic testing [nei_020_chunk_03].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.
